roadmap.goal: Slice 01 (ADO #5692), ADR-137: a prospect who opens Lighthouse inside Jira signs in at top level against the identity provider that instance already uses, and the frame that comes back is theirs — their own name, their own permissions, including the ones that reach them only through a group mapping. A viewer who signs in and holds nothing is told so rather than shown an empty rectangle. Deleting that person ends their live frame within one request, without quietly re-creating the profile an administrator just removed. The API-key embed path stays MINTABLE alongside it, which is the only thing that makes the ordering reversible. Turn 15 already-authored RED backend tests green, un-ignore one more, author exactly two new tests, and delete nothing.
roadmap.overview: UNUSUAL SHAPE, and it is the second time this repository has run it: DISTILL has already written every acceptance test and this roadmap plans NO test authoring except two owed concurrency properties that could not be written before the repository method they probe existed. Unlike slice 04 of epic 5513, there are NO SCAFFOLDS — DISTILL touched no production code at all. Every test enters through HTTP, where a missing endpoint is a runtime 404 rather than a build break, and the two storage tests use raw SQL against the migrated schema, where a missing column is a caught DbException folded into a boolean. That is why the suite compiles at zero warnings while sixteen of its assertions are unsatisfied. Backbone, in the order the three hops imply: 01-01 the schema learns that an outcome can be a refusal (the migration, FIRST and non-negotiable) -> 01-02 hop 1, the sign-in tab decides and records (4 red) -> 01-03 hop 2, the outcome travels back exactly once and everything else is one answer (6 red) -> 01-04 hop 3, the frame is entered as the viewer and stays theirs only while they exist (5 red) -> 01-05 the group-mapped viewer sees the same team inside the frame as outside it (1 red, and it is the slice's whole hypothesis) -> 01-06 the two owed single-use properties under concurrency on a real provider (2 authored) -> 01-07 the walking skeleton through real Keycloak plus both Postgres halves, and the slice closes. THE FIRST STEP IS THE MIGRATION AND IT IS WHERE THE SLICE IS MOST LIKELY TO GO WRONG SILENTLY: EF cannot add a check constraint to an existing SQLite table with ALTER TABLE, so it emits a table REBUILD, and a rebuild of a table carrying OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade) on a foreign key that is simultaneously becoming optional is the exact concrete shape of the peer review's only HIGH finding. Scenario 21 is green today on purpose and is the guard; if it reds after the migration, the migration ate ADR-131's revocation lever 1. TWO DESIGN GAPS THIS ROADMAP RESOLVES RATHER THAN INHERITS, both of which land in step 01-01 because both change the migration: (a) D55 says the nonce hash is CLEARED on consumption, but D62/scenario 12 require a second read of a consumed nonce to be recognisable — clearing the hash destroys the only way to recognise it, so a fourth nullable column HandshakeConsumedAt is added and the conditional update keys on it instead; (b) D53's cascade re-declaration and the SQLite rebuild together will trip ExpandOnlyMigrationGuardTest, which is a textual scan for DropTable/RenameTable in an Up method. Both are written up in 01-01's implementation_notes with the recommended resolution and the reason it is a decision rather than a detail.

steps.implementation_notes:
FIRST, AND NOT NEGOTIABLE — every other step needs these columns, and the two storage tests read raw SQL against the migrated schema, so nothing in this slice is testable until the migration exists. GENERATE IT WITH `Lighthouse.Backend/Create-Migration.ps1 -MigrationName <name>`, NEVER `dotnet ef migrations add` directly: the script generates BOTH provider assemblies against a throwaway Postgres container and cleans up after itself, and a migration present in only one assembly breaks every real-provider test in the suite. THREE THINGS TO GET RIGHT BEFORE RUNNING IT, because all three change the generated file and none is recoverable without a second migration.

(1) THE CASCADE. `LighthouseAppContext.cs:166-170` currently declares `.OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade)` on a REQUIRED FK. Making `ApiKeyId` an `int?` flips EF's default to `ClientSetNull`, and a crafter who changes the property and moves on deletes ADR-131's revocation lever 1 during the one slice where both paths still run, with no failing test anywhere. Re-declare `.OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade)` EXPLICITLY on the now-optional relationship. Scenario 21 is green today on purpose and is the guard — run it before and after.

(2) A FOURTH COLUMN THE DESIGN DOES NOT LIST, AND WHY. D52 names three added columns; D55 says nonce consumption CLEARS `HandshakeNonceHash`. Those two together make D62/scenario 12 IMPOSSIBLE: once the hash is cleared, a second read of that nonce finds no row and is indistinguishable from an unknown nonce, so there is nothing to recognise and nothing to log, and `ASecondReadOfAConsumedNonce_IsRecordedAsAnAnomaly` can never pass. The resolution this roadmap takes: add `HandshakeConsumedAt` (DateTime?) and DO NOT clear the hash. The conditional update's predicate becomes `HandshakeNonceHash == hash AND HandshakeConsumedAt == null AND ExpiresAt > now`, which preserves D55's atomicity argument exactly — the affected-row count still yields one winner and N-1 losers — while leaving the row findable by a second reader. D45 is unharmed: the second reader still receives the byte-identical pending response (scenario 11 asserts equality of the four readings, not that a consumed nonce is unfindable). This is an AMENDMENT to D55's literal wording, taken here because it lands in the migration; say so in the commit body and flag it for the maintainer rather than letting it read as a detail. The storage tests' INSERT statements name their columns explicitly, so a fourth nullable column does not disturb them.

(3) THE EXPAND-ONLY GUARD WILL PROBABLY FIRE, AND THAT IS NOT A REASON TO BUMP THE BASELINE. SQLite cannot add a check constraint to an existing table with ALTER TABLE, so EF emits a table REBUILD: `CreateTable(ef_temp_EmbedSessionTokens)` -> `Sql(INSERT INTO ... SELECT)` -> `DropTable(EmbedSessionTokens)` -> `RenameTable(ef_temp_... -> EmbedSessionTokens)`. `ExpandOnlyMigrationGuardTest.RealMigrations_AddedAfterBaseline_AreAdditiveOnly` is a TEXTUAL scan of every migration Up() for DropTable/RenameTable/DropColumn, so it will report the rebuild as destructive. It is not: a rebuild preserves every column and every row, and the guard's stated purpose — old pods never depend on a dropped column during a rolling update — is untouched by it. RECOMMENDED RESOLUTION: narrow `ExpandOnlyMigrationGuard` to recognise the EF SQLite rebuild pattern (a DropTable/RenameTable pair whose names pair with an `ef_temp_` CreateTable in the same Up) rather than bumping `ExpandOnlyBaselineTimestamp`, which would blind the guard to every genuinely destructive migration between the baseline and now. Whichever you choose, the three synthetic guard tests in that fixture must stay green and the choice goes in the commit body. VERIFY THE REBUILD'S FOREIGN KEY BY READING THE GENERATED SQLITE MIGRATION: the SPIKE's DQ-3 probe used `EnsureCreated`, not a migration, so the rebuild's `ON DELETE` clause is EXPECTED, NOT VERIFIED. Read it, then let scenario 21 prove it.

NULLABILITY FALLOUT, which is the whole of the compile-keeping edits: `TokenId` and `SecretHash` become `string?`, `ApiKeyId` becomes `int?`. `EmbedSessionTokenService.RedeemAsync` compares against `stored.SecretHash` and returns `stored.ApiKeyId`; `EmbedEntryController` passes `redemption.ApiKeyId` to `ResolveByApiKeyId(int)`. Keep those paths behaving EXACTLY as they do today for an API-key-minted row — a null-guard that returns the existing refusal, never a widening. ZERO null-forgiving `!` anywhere: S8969/S8970 are ERROR severity since SonarAnalyzer.CSharp 10.30 and break the build, not just the gate. Security review F7 applies to the new `Subject` guard as it lands: the empty-string analogue of a zero id is not protected by a database sequence, so an empty or whitespace subject must be refused explicitly and the justification must read `defence in depth, retained deliberately`, never `equivalent`.

MODEL CONFIGURATION: `HasCheckConstraint` goes on `ToTable(t => t.HasCheckConstraint("CK_EmbedSessionTokens_GrantOrRefusal", ...))` and the name is a CONTRACT (D65) — the test reads it out of `sqlite_master` and `pg_constraint` by that exact string. Index `HandshakeNonceHash` and index `Subject`; both are looked up on every poll and every framed request respectively. `Subject` is deliberately NOT a foreign key to `UserProfile` — profiles are created lazily by two different writers, so an FK would couple a credential's lifetime to a row this design does not own. Do not `.IsRequired()` any added column.

CI LEDGER RULES THAT BITE HERE: a new property on a persisted model needs a migration and InMemory tests never catch the gap; no non-default sentinel on a bool column; a persisted DAY key is DateOnly, never DateTime — `HandshakeConsumedAt` is an INSTANT, not a day, so DateTime is correct and it must be written from the injected TimeProvider, never `DateTime.UtcNow.Date` or `DateTime.Today`. Generated migration files carry pre-existing CA1861 hits and are ledger noise; filter the analyzer sweep to the files you actually hand-edited.

steps.name: Hop 1 — the sign-in tab decides, and Lighthouse writes down what it decided
criteria: An unauthenticated arrival is sent to the identity provider's own authorization endpoint, explicitly, by name. Falling through to the cookie scheme's forwarded challenge lands the viewer on the SPA login page, which is the blank rectangle at top level and the exact mistake this hop exists to avoid

Only a principal authenticated on the ordinary session cookie counts as signed in. Everything else — an embed cookie, an API key, a bearer token — is CHALLENGED rather than refused, so an embed-cookie-only caller completes an ordinary login and ends up holding a real session, which is the outcome we wanted anyway

A signed-in viewer who holds no readable scope produces exactly one row recording the refusal, and that row holds no token id and no secret a redemption could ever match. The decision is a question asked of the permission model, which mutates nothing; the row is a single insert that records the answer

A request with no nonce is refused before any identity provider is involved. Bouncing a viewer through a login to discover afterwards that there was nowhere to put the answer is a worse failure than a fast refusal

The embed surface is invisible on an instance whose authentication is off, and invisible on an instance whose authentication cannot work. The availability question is answered BEFORE any authentication scheme is looked up — which is the ordering that converts the ignored test into a real assertion instead of an exception

The trust anchor still holds: the forged interactive cookie is still read as a real Lighthouse session. If it stops being one, every failure below this step is a setup failure wearing the costume of a product failure
steps.implementation_notes:
THE TRAP THAT WILL COST A SESSION IF IT IS NOT READ FIRST — D64, found by DISTILL while making the test RED. The signed-in predicate is `await HttpContext.AuthenticateAsync(SmartAuthSchemeSelector.CookieScheme)` and its `.Succeeded`. It is NOT `User.Identity.AuthenticationType == SmartAuthSchemeSelector.CookieScheme`. After a real OIDC login the OIDC handler BUILDS the identity and signs it into the cookie scheme, so the identity reads `OpenIdConnect` and only the TICKET names `Cookies`. The obvious check therefore refuses every genuine interactive session, and it fails as a SILENT CHALLENGE LOOP rather than as an exception — the viewer bounces through the identity provider forever and no test throws. `ViewerEmbedTestHost.ForgeInteractiveSessionCookie` deliberately mirrors production here (identity type `OpenIdConnect`, ticket scheme `Cookies`), so a wrong check fails scenario 7 and passes nothing.

F2 IS WHAT THE POSITIVE PHRASING BUYS. State the guard positively — only CookieScheme counts — rather than as an exclusion of embed cookies. An embed cookie satisfies a bare `[Authorize]`, and if that were enough a session would mint its own successor forever and ADR-130's 30-minute non-sliding bound would be unbounded. Phrased positively, an embed-cookie-only caller is challenged, logs in, and arrives with a real session; F2 closes by construction rather than by a check that could be forgotten.

ORDER INSIDE THE ACTION, and it is the whole of criterion 5: (1) resolve AuthMode and return 404 for anything that is not Enabled and 403 for Blocked, EXACTLY as `EmbedSessionController.IsEmbedSurfaceAvailable` does and for the recorded reason — the embed cookie scheme is not registered when authentication is disabled, so `[Authorize(AuthenticationSchemes = ...)]` would pre-empt the 404; (2) validate the nonce (present, well-formed) and 400 otherwise; (3) `AuthenticateAsync(CookieScheme)` and `Challenge(OpenIdConnectDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)` with `RedirectUri` set to this same path INCLUDING the nonce, naming the scheme EXPLICITLY — scenario 8 asserts the redirect starts with the identity provider's authorization endpoint, so a forwarded challenge to `/Account/Login` fails it and the assertion exists precisely to catch that; (4) resolve the viewer's profile; (5) ask RBAC; (6) write one row; (7) render the terminal page. PROFILE RESOLUTION HERE IS A DECLARED WRITE, AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF D57. `/embed/start` MUST create the profile — scenario 19 asserts a first-time viewer appears in the administrator's user list — so `ICurrentUserProfileService.GetOrCreateFromPrincipalAsync` is the RIGHT service AT THIS SEAM and the WRONG one in the validator (01-04). Two different seams, two opposite answers; conflating them is easy and only one of the two has a test that catches it.

THE RBAC QUESTION IS READ-ONLY AND MUST STAY THAT WAY. Add ONE method to `IRbacAdministrationService` — `HasAnyReadableScopeAsync(ClaimsPrincipal, CancellationToken)` — returning a bool over the effective-permission map the service already builds privately, with RBAC enforcement taken into account. `UserAuthorizationSummary` is NOT the source: it carries only ADMIN rights (AdminTeamIds, AdminPortfolioIds, IsSystemAdmin) and a pure viewer would be refused wrongly. `GetReadableTeamIdsAsync`/`GetReadablePortfolioIdsAsync` are semantically right but enumerate every id to answer a yes/no. Do not inline the permission logic into the write path — a crafter who does makes the decision untestable without a database, and the two are separated in the design on purpose.

THE WRITE. One insert carrying Subject, the HASHED nonce (same digest discipline as SecretHash — a database read must not yield a live credential), and either (TokenId + SecretHash, RefusalCode null) or (RefusalCode, both null). Reuse the existing `GenerateUrlSafeValue`/`HashSecret` helpers rather than adding a second hashing site. `ExpiresAt` at this point is the OUTCOME window, not the token window — see 01-03, which rewrites it at consumption. The row is written at RESOLUTION and never before (D51); there is no pre-registration and no unauthenticated write endpoint.

THE TERMINAL PAGE (D61/D66). Two `const string` documents in the controller, same shape as `EmbedEntryController.RefusalHtml` — one document, no subresources, one sentence of instruction — with an `<h1>` of EXACTLY `You are signed in to Lighthouse` or `Lighthouse has nothing to show you`. These strings are pinned in `EmbedEntryPage.GRANT_HEADING`/`REFUSAL_HEADING` and NO BACKEND TEST ASSERTS THEM: only the E2E in 01-07 catches a mismatch, so get them byte-right now.

CONFIGURATION (DQ-2, first half). Add `HandshakeOutcomeLifetimeSeconds` to `EmbedConfiguration` defaulting to 300 and use it for the row's `ExpiresAt`. Do NOT reuse `TokenLifetimeSeconds` (60s): the token's window is bounded by MACHINE latency — one redirect — while the outcome's is bounded by HUMAN latency and must survive a login behind a password manager or an MFA prompt. Under a shared 60s the poll returns pending after a slow login and the Jira page says `try again` for a sign-in that worked, intermittently and only for the slowest users, which is the worst possible distribution. THE NUMBER 300 IS PROPOSED, NOT RATIFIED, and nobody has measured the Forge resolver's real poll interval — flag it for the maintainer.

REFUSAL VOCABULARY (DQ-1). Proposed closed set: `no_access`, `auth_unavailable`, `instance_unavailable`. No test pins any string — scenarios 6 and 19 assert only that a refusalCode is PRESENT — so this is settleable without touching a test. S14 requires the vocabulary to be small, closed and class-level: it must name the CLASS of refusal, never the reason in prose, and never anything about who the viewer is or what the instance contains. NOTE THE INCONSISTENCY BEFORE ADOPTING THE THIRD CODE: DQ-1 justifies `instance_unavailable` by the Blocked licence state, but scenario 15 has BOTH endpoints answer 403 for Blocked, so no row and no refusal code is ever produced for it and the Jira page infers that state from the status. Either the third code has a different justification or it is not needed yet — decide, and say which in the commit body.

ROUTING AND POLICY: `[Route("embed")]`, `[ApiController]`, `[AllowAnonymous]`, OUTSIDE `/api` on purpose — an `/api` challenge becomes a bare 401, which is the blank rectangle D26 exists to prevent. `[EnableRateLimiting(RateLimitingConfiguration.EmbedSessionPolicy)]` on the action; the shipped-config guard test loops over the policy constants, so the endpoint inherits F1's second ask for free. Set `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` as the entry point already does — the nonce rides the query string and must not travel onward.

steps.name: Hop 2 — the outcome travels back exactly once, and everything else is one answer
criteria: A nonce that matches an unconsumed grant returns the token and its expiry, and the nonce is spent in the same breath. A nonce that matches an unconsumed refusal returns the refusal class, and is spent the same way — the Jira page has to be able to stop polling and say something true, which is the whole reason the refusal travels the grant's channel

Unknown, not-yet-resolved, already-consumed and malformed nonces are ONE identical response — identical to each other, not merely similar. Making them equal by making them all the same failure is a legitimate implementation; making them differ is not, because a channel that answers `a session happened here` is an oracle for live sessions

The second reader of a spent nonce is recorded as an anomaly under a stable event name, while still receiving the same indistinguishable answer as everyone else. This prevents nothing and is not a control: it converts an invisible impersonation into a visible one, on both sides, for the cost of one log line and one branch

Two callers cannot both win. Consumption is the database's decision, expressed as an affected-row count, not a read followed by a write that passes every single-threaded test and hands out a second credential exactly when it matters

The expiry the poll hands back is the one redemption actually enforces. A window advertised in the response and a different window enforced in storage is a lie that only shows up as an intermittent failure for slow signers-in
The handshake is invisible when authentication is off and blocked when the licence is not valid, in the same two answers the sign-in hop gives, so the embed surface has one rule rather than two
A viewer who signs in for the first time appears in the administrator's user list AND is refused — the declared effect of resolving a viewer, asserted rather than left to be discovered by a customer
steps.implementation_notes:
READ SCENARIO 11 BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING. It compares four `HandshakeReading` records for EQUALITY, and that record carries BOTH the status code and the body — so pending, unknown, expired, consumed and malformed must agree on both. DISTILL wrote it that way on purpose: it pins the PROPERTY without pinning the wire shape, so 404-with-empty-body and 200-with-an-empty-object are both legitimate implementations and the choice is yours. Pick one, and note in the commit body that scenarios 14 and 15 constrain the OTHER two statuses (404 for Disabled, 403 for Blocked), so a pending shape of 404 makes `authentication is off` and `your sign-in has not finished` indistinguishable to the Forge page — which is not a security problem but IS a usability one the resolver has to live with. 200-with-a-bare-object keeps those three distinguishable and is the recommended reading. `neverIssued.HasProperty("token")` and `HasProperty("refusalCode")` must both be false, so the pending body must not carry either key even as null.

CONSUMPTION IS THE CONDITIONAL UPDATE, AND 01-01 ALREADY DECIDED ITS SHAPE. `ExecuteUpdateAsync` over `Where(HandshakeNonceHash == hash && HandshakeConsumedAt == null && ExpiresAt > now)`, setting `HandshakeConsumedAt = now` AND — this is the DQ-2 half nobody has written down — setting `ExpiresAt = now + TokenLifetimeSeconds` for a GRANT row. That single rewrite is what makes criterion 5 true: the row's `ExpiresAt` starts as the 300-second OUTCOME window (so a slow human login still resolves) and becomes the 60-second TOKEN window at the instant the frame learns about it (so ADR-131's redemption bound is the one actually enforced, since `TryMarkRedeemedAsync` gates on `ExpiresAt > redeemedAt`). Without it the token is redeemable for the whole outcome window and the `expiresAt` the poll advertises is a fiction. Do NOT do this with a read-then-write; the affected-row count is the atomicity and it is the same shape `TryMarkRedeemedAsync` already uses. Require EXACTLY one affected row; a zero means someone else won, or it never existed, or it expired — and all three produce the same answer, which is the point.

D62 / SCENARIO 12 — HOW THE REPLAY IS EVEN DETECTABLE. Because 01-01 kept the nonce hash rather than clearing it, a second poll can still FIND the row and see `HandshakeConsumedAt != null`. That is the only reason this branch exists. Emit `LogWarning` with `EventId.Name = "EmbedHandshakeNonceReplayed"` — the test asserts on the NAME, not the message, because the message will be rewritten and the name is the stable surface. Log the event and then return THE SAME pending response as everyone else: observability must not become the oracle D45 forbids. DQ-4's shape question (a log line versus a first-class security event) is still the maintainer's; the codebase has no security-event channel and introducing one for a single event builds the abstraction before the second caller. N1 carries: there is still no token or nonce redaction, so a single config edit can write live credentials to ./logs/ — do not log the nonce or its hash.

WHAT THE GRANT RESPONSE CARRIES, AND WHAT IT MUST NOT. `{ token, expiresAt }` and nothing else. NO absolute URL: F5's `BuildEmbedUrl` reflected Host and Scheme and is retired by deletion; the Forge side composes the entry URL from the `targetInstance` it already stores, which is the security review's own preferred remedy. The refusal response carries `{ refusalCode }` and nothing else — S14 forbids prose, forbids anything about who the viewer is, and forbids anything about what the instance contains.

ROUTING. `[Route("api/v1/embed")]` plus `[Route("api/latest/embed")]` to match the house convention, `[ApiController]`, `[AllowAnonymous]`, `[HttpGet("handshake/{nonce}")]`. `EmbedSessionController` already owns `api/v1/embed` with `[Authorize]` — a SECOND controller on the same prefix is correct and deliberate here, because the action templates differ (`handshake/{nonce}` versus `session-token`) and it keeps `[AllowAnonymous]` off the minting controller. Do NOT add the anonymous action to `EmbedSessionController`. Same AuthMode-first ordering as 01-02, same `EmbedSessionPolicy` rate limiting — and note S7's caveat honestly: the limiter partitions on client IP, is per-instance and in-memory, so with N replicas an attacker gets roughly N x 20. Against a 256-bit nonce that is irrelevant, which is exactly the point: entropy is the control and rate limiting is depth.

THE RESOLVER HOLDS NO CREDENTIAL AND GETS EXACTLY ONE VERB. No write port is exposed to it — it cannot create, revoke or mutate anything. That is a stronger read/write split than the API-key design achieved, where the same caller could mint and revoke, and it is worth not eroding for convenience.

PRUNING. `MintAsync` opportunistically calls `PruneSpentAsync` and a refusal row is never redeemed, so it survives until expiry. Be aware that pruning inside the handshake path could delete a consumed-and-expired row and silently stop the replay event firing for it; that is outside every test's window and acceptable, but say so rather than discovering it during an incident.

CI LEDGER RULES THAT BITE HERE: CA1859 (concrete types on every new non-public member, parameters included); S6964 — value-type properties on a bound DTO must be nullable or binding silently defaults them; ASP0015 on well-known headers; SYSLIB1045 — nonce validation is a length-and-alphabet check, not a regex; S8969/S8970 — zero `!`; S3776 on the action, which now has at least five branches. ASP.NET Core `[FromRoute]`/`[FromQuery]` parameters are REQUIRED by default under nullable-enabled C# (ledger, 2026-05-16) — a malformed-nonce path that must return the pending shape rather than a framework 400 needs the parameter typed `string?` and validated in the body.

steps.name: Hop 3 — the frame is entered as the viewer, and stays theirs only while they exist
criteria: A redeemed token establishes a session for the PERSON who signed in, not for a key's owner, and the frame it opens carries exactly what that person may read — and nothing else. A frame that shows more than the viewer's own scope is the failure the refusal path exists to prevent, arriving through the opposite door

Deleting the viewer ends their live frame within ONE request, rather than within the cookie's remaining lifetime. There is no deactivation in this product; deletion is the control, and any wording that promises otherwise describes a feature that does not exist

Rejecting a deleted viewer does not bring their profile back. The request after the rejection must be refused too — a lookup that creates would resurrect the profile on the first rejection and authenticate the second, turning the whole control into a no-op that looks like it works, on that person's very next request and with every other test still passing

The port the validator is handed cannot write. Not `should not`: the interface offers no create method, so the resurrection above is not something a later reader can reintroduce by picking the convenient service off the container

An embed cookie still cannot start a handshake, now proven through the whole loop rather than at the endpoint alone: a genuine embed session, presented to the sign-in hop, is challenged and is granted no successor. Otherwise the thirty-minute bound is unbounded

When both cookies arrive on one request, the person's own login wins. Opening an embed link at top level puts them in the same jar, and there a single clicked link must not silently replace who someone is

The API-key redemption path behaves exactly as it did before — same refusal on an unresolvable owner, same redirect, same cookie. Slice 01 keeps it mintable, and that is the only thing making the ordering reversible

THE ENTRY POINT AND THE VALIDATOR ARE ONE STEP ON PURPOSE, and splitting them will produce a step that cannot go green. The shipped validator rejects any principal without an `api_key_id` claim; a viewer principal correctly carries none, so the moment the entry point builds one, EVERY framed request is rejected until the validator is reworked. There is no ordering of two smaller steps that leaves the suite green in between.

D57 IS THE TRAP AND IT HAS A TEST THAT LOOKS LIKE IT PASSES EITHER WAY UNTIL YOU READ IT. `ICurrentUserProfileService.GetOrCreateFromPrincipalAsync` CREATES. Calling it from the validator re-creates the profile an administrator just deleted, on that person's very next request, and scenario 17 — delete, then one request, expect 401 — STILL PASSES, because the resurrection happens during the request that is being rejected. Scenario 18 is the mirror that catches it by issuing a SECOND request and requiring 401 again. Create `IUserProfileLookup` with EXACTLY ONE METHOD — find a UserProfile (or its display name) by subject — and NO create method ON THE INTERFACE. A port that only reads must not offer a write; that is the whole point, and `CountProfiles` was deliberately deleted from the test host on review so that the control is observed at the port rather than against the schema. `UserProfile.Subject` already carries a unique index (`LighthouseAppContext.cs:103-105`), so the lookup is one indexed row with `AsNoTracking()`. Note the deliberate asymmetry with 01-02: `/embed/start` MUST create (scenario 19), the validator MUST NOT. Two seams, opposite answers.

THE VALIDATOR STAYS A NAMED PRIVATE STATIC METHOD IN Program.cs. Do NOT inline it as a lambda in `ConfigureAuthentication`: ci-learnings 2026-08-04 records a five-line `OnValidatePrincipal` lambda taking that method's cognitive complexity from 15 to 17 with no other edit, and S3776 is a Sonar-gate failure invisible to `dotnet build`. Rename it to something honest — it no longer only checks a key — and give it BOTH branches: a principal carrying `api_key_id` resolves through `IApiKeyIdentityResolver` exactly as today (the API-key path stays reachable), a principal carrying `sub` resolves through `IUserProfileLookup`, and a principal carrying NEITHER is rejected. That third case is explicit in the reuse analysis and is what stops a malformed principal falling through open.

THE PRINCIPAL. Add a SECOND overload to `ApiKeyPrincipalFactory` beside the key overload: `(subject, displayName, authenticationScheme) -> ClaimsPrincipal` carrying `sub`, `name` and `auth_method=embed`. Add an `AuthMethodEmbedValue` const next to the existing `AuthMethodValue`. The class stays STATIC and PURE — no repository, no clock, no HttpContext — because that purity is what keeps the claims-parity assertion a statement about a function rather than about a request. The name is wrong on purpose now (D63) and does not change this release. `auth_method=embed` is what 01-05 gates on; without it that step has nothing to read.

REDEMPTION CARRIES A SUBJECT NOW. `EmbedSessionTokenRedemption` gains the subject alongside the (now nullable) ApiKeyId, and the entry point branches: subject present -> build the viewer principal; ApiKeyId present -> the existing `ResolveByApiKeyId` path, INCLUDING its `OwnerResolutionState != Resolved` refusal and its warning log, unchanged. Everything else in `EmbedEntryController` is correct and STAYS: the `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` header, the AuthMode 404, the clean-URL 302 that gets the token out of the address bar immediately, `Url.IsLocalUrl` on `returnPath` with all its negative tests, the uniform refusal HTML and the uniform 401. F7 applies to the new branch: an empty or whitespace subject must be refused EXPLICITLY, and the justification reads `defence in depth, retained deliberately`, never `equivalent`. The redirect still happens AFTER the authenticated cookie is set — do not reorder it.

WHAT MUST NOT CHANGE. `SmartAuthSchemeSelector` is REUSED AS-IS, UNMODIFIED: F4's precedence inversion at lines 54-66 is already shipped and is exactly what scenario 10 asserts. The embed cookie scheme block in `Program.cs:694-723` is REUSED AS-IS: ADR-130 in full, including `Cookie.Extensions.Add("Partitioned")`, and the existing wire assertion on the literal Set-Cookie header — both halves — carries over untouched. `DisabledAuthenticationHandler` is still the tempting shortcut, still hands every anonymous caller a session, and is now worse because the identity attached would be a PERSON's rather than a key's.

criteria: A viewer whose ONLY access comes from a group-to-role mapping resolves the same team inside the frame as they do in an ordinary browser tab. The stored group snapshot is consulted for principals that STRUCTURALLY cannot carry live group claims, named as such, rather than for principals that happen to carry a particular credential id. The predicate names the real condition instead of a proxy for it

THE SMALLEST DIFF IN THE SLICE AND THE ONE THE WHOLE WAVE EXISTS TO CATCH. One conjunct, in the most security-sensitive method in the codebase. `RbacAdministrationService.GetVirtualPermissionsAsync:1093` currently reads `if (groupValues.Count == 0 && TryGetApiKeyId(principal, out _))`. Re-gate it on the AUTHENTICATION METHOD: the fallback applies when `auth_method` is `api-key` OR `embed`, not when an `api_key_id` claim happens to be present. Reuse `ApiKeyPrincipalFactory.AuthMethodClaimType` and its two value constants rather than string literals — S1192 and, more importantly, the claim type is the shared contract between this method and 01-04's factory.

WHY THIS IS A DESIGN AND NOT A PATCH, so nobody softens it later. A viewer-identity embed principal carries `sub` and, CORRECTLY, no `api_key_id`; it also carries no group claims, because it is rebuilt from a stored subject rather than from a live token. So `groupValues.Count == 0` is true, `TryGetApiKeyId` is false, the snapshot is not loaded, and `virtualPermissions` is empty. A viewer whose entire Lighthouse access comes from a group mapping resolves ZERO permissions inside the frame while working perfectly in an ordinary tab. It fails CLOSED, so nothing errors — the frame is simply empty, which is the blank-rectangle failure this epic exists to prevent, arriving one layer deeper than anyone anticipated. Worse: the refusal decision at `/embed/start` runs under the INTERACTIVE principal, which does carry live group claims, so Lighthouse would decide GRANT and the session that grant authorises would resolve nothing — the refusal decision and the session it authorises evaluating different permission sets, which is precisely the class of mistake the refusal was written to prevent. And the snapshot is FRESH BY CONSTRUCTION: hop 1 IS an OIDC sign-in, so `WriteGroupSnapshotOnTokenValidatedAsync` (Program.cs:749-796) writes the snapshot the framed session reads minutes later. The staleness argument that would apply to an API-key principal — whose owner may not have logged in for months — does not apply here at all.

WHY IT IS NOT A FAIL-OPEN WIDENING, which is the thing a reviewer will and should ask. An ordinary OIDC cookie principal has NO `auth_method` claim at all, so it never reaches the fallback and its behaviour is byte-identical to today. Scenario 5 asserts exactly that against a profile that DOES carry a snapshot, so it is not vacuous. It is green today: if it goes red here, the conjunct was widened rather than re-aimed.

THE UNIT TEST THIS STEP OWES (DISTILL pre-requisite 3). Scenario 5 covers the ordinary-principal-unchanged half through HTTP; the unit level is where a mutation survivor shows, because the HTTP path has many reasons to return an empty team list and only one of them is this conjunct. Add ONE case to the existing `RbacAdministrationServiceTest` fixture, in that fixture's existing idiom, asserting that a principal with no `auth_method` claim and a profile carrying a snapshot resolves no group-mapped rule. Do not invent a new test host. NUnit1028: any helper you add is `private static`, and making it non-public ARMS CA1859, so give it a concrete return type in the same edit.

DO NOT TOUCH `LoadOwnerGroupSnapshotAsync`. It reads `sub` off the principal and both principal shapes carry it; the method needs no change and changing it widens the blast radius of this step from one conjunct to two methods. `TryGetApiKeyId` stays — the API-key path still uses it elsewhere and slice 03 is where anything gets deleted.

PROPERTY 1, THE NONCE. SANITY-CHECK BOTH PROPERTIES BEFORE BELIEVING THEM (ci-learnings: after writing any assertion whose failure you have not seen, sabotage the production code and re-run it). Replace the conditional update with a read-then-write, confirm the winner count goes above one, then restore. `if (false)` does NOT work for this in C# — `TreatWarningsAsErrors` turns CS0162 unreachable-code into a build error — so change the predicate, do not comment it out. A concurrency test that has never gone red is a test that has never run its race.

CI LEDGER RULES THAT BITE HERE, and this file is exactly where they bite: NUnit4002 — `Is.Zero`, never `Is.EqualTo(0)`, and it is a PRE-COMMIT HARD BLOCK; NUnit2046 — `Has.Count.EqualTo(N)` on a collection, never `Assert.That(x.Count, ...)`; NUnit2056 — `using (Assert.EnterMultipleScope())`, never `Assert.Multiple(...)`; CA1861 — no inline `new[] {...}` in an assertion, hoist to a `static readonly` field, and the hook has been observed to MISS this three times, so re-grep `Is\.\w*\(new\[\]` by hand; NUnit1028 — every non-[Test] member is `private static`, which then ARMS CA1859, so give it a concrete type in the same edit. Run `dotnet format analyzers` over this file specifically before committing.

steps.implementation_notes:
LAST BECAUSE IT IS THE ONLY TEST THAT PROVES THE WHOLE CHAIN AT ONCE, AND THE EXPECTATION IS ZERO PRODUCTION CHANGE HERE. If 01-02 through 01-05 are right, the skeleton goes green when they land. The two controllers are listed because they are where a fix would go — and a change needed at this step is a signal that a hop got something wrong, not a licence to special-case the skeleton. The E2E needs NO new page-object work: `EmbedEntryPage` already has START_PATH, GRANT_HEADING, REFUSAL_HEADING, `openSignInTab`, `signInCompleteHeading`, `noAccessHeading` and `refusalHeading`, and `LighthousePage` already has `overviewLink` and `currentUserDisplay`.

RUN IT YOURSELF, LOCALLY, AGAINST A LIVE LIGHTHOUSE. The house rule is explicit: never commit a Playwright spec or page object you have not run. The spec is already committed, so what this step owes is the RUN. It is `@auth`-tagged and serial, and its first case uploads a premium licence as a precondition. Hop 1 needs a real identity provider over real HTTPS — the auth-enabled instance is the only place the flow runs at all — so if the local auth stack is not up, this step is blocked on infrastructure rather than on code, and saying so is better than reporting a skeleton that never ran. One engine only; Chrome and Safari remain unrun across this whole epic and that is recorded, not hidden.

THE HEADING IS THE ONE THING ONLY THIS STEP CAN CATCH (criterion 4). `EmbedEntryPage.GRANT_HEADING` is `You are signed in to Lighthouse` and `REFUSAL_HEADING` is `Lighthouse has nothing to show you`. No integration test asserts either — they assert status 200 — so a typo in the controller's `const string` ships silently until here. `getByRole("heading", { name })` is a case-insensitive substring match, so a heading that merely CONTAINS the expected text passes; read the rendered page, do not only read the green tick.

THE POSTGRES HALVES NEED DOCKER and are `[Category("requires-docker")]`. Run them explicitly — they do not run in the default local pass, which is exactly how a provider-specific constraint failure reaches CI. The Postgres cascade case is the one that would tell you 01-01's SQLite table rebuild hid a `ClientSetNull` on one provider only.

MUTATION TESTING. No Stryker config is committed in this repo and `.gitignore` excludes `**/stryker-config*.json` as deliberate policy, so write one from scratch; the reproducible backend config for this epic is recorded in feature-delta.md around L1793-1832. `coverage-analysis: perTest` is not optional — without it Stryker runs the full suite per mutant and is unusably slow. Two recorded traps: Stryker.NET IGNORES `{a..b}` line-span syntax AND whole-file `mutate` globs via both the config file and the `-m` CLI flag, which is how a run ends up producing 13547 mutants across the whole backend; and Stryker.NET has no test filter, so any `requires-docker` category executes inside the mutation loop. Aim it at the two new controllers, the two new service methods and the repository's conditional update. JUDGE SURVIVORS: an equivalent mutant gets a WRITTEN REASON, not an invented test asserting an implementation detail. Expect survivors in the terminal-page copy — the ledger's single most common survivor is a test that compares a value to the constant it came from, and here the copy is pinned only in the E2E page object; if blanking a heading to the empty string survives, that is a real gap and the fix is a backend assertion on the literal, not a shrug.

BEFORE THE PUSH, IN THIS ORDER: `cd Lighthouse.Backend && dotnet format analyzers Lighthouse.sln --severity info --verify-no-changes --no-restore`, filtered to the files this slice hand-edited (generated migrations carry ~35 pre-existing CA1861 hits and are noise); then `dotnet build` at zero warnings; then the full `dotnet test`, with the green bar being `everything except the two LicenseServiceTest cases that also fail at main`. The Sonar gate runs on pushes to `main` too, not only on pull requests, and a batch of unpushed feature commits is judged as one diff the moment it lands.

WHAT SHIPPING THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH, and it belongs in the commit body so nobody reads the green suite as more than it is: nothing Forge — no modal, no `router.open`, no resolver, no nested frame, no partitioned cookie in a genuinely cross-site context; the Forge-side bounded timeout; and K1 is still 0. This is a better demo, not demand evidence. The unauthenticated-handshake residual travels forward as an OPEN item, not a settled one.

walking_skeleton.contract_assertion: Two assertions make this non-fakeable. Second, the differential pair in scenario 2 at integration level: the frame contains the team this viewer may read AND NOT the team they may not. A frame that shows everything passes the first assertion and fails the second, which is why the fixture holds two viewers and two teams.

risks.risk: The migration silently converts ADR-131's revocation lever 1 into a no-op. Making ApiKeyId optional flips EF's default from Cascade to ClientSetNull, and EF's SQLite table REBUILD (forced because SQLite cannot ALTER TABLE a check constraint into existence) is a second, independent way the same ON DELETE clause can be lost. Both happen inside a migration that is genuinely additive, so the expand-only guard cannot see either — it guards schema shape, and this is a behaviour change wearing an additive one.
risks.mitigation: Scenario 21 is authored, green today on purpose, and named as 01-01's must-stay-green guard on both providers. 01-01's notes require re-declaring the cascade explicitly AND reading the generated SQLite migration's ON DELETE clause by eye, because the SPIKE's DQ-3 probe used EnsureCreated rather than a migration and therefore never exercised a rebuild. 01-07 re-runs the Postgres half, which is where a one-provider divergence would show.

risks.risk: D55 and D62 contradict each other and nobody noticed until this roadmap. D55 says nonce consumption CLEARS HandshakeNonceHash; D62 and scenario 12 require the second reader of a consumed nonce to be recognised and logged. Once the hash is cleared the row is unfindable, so the replay is indistinguishable from an unknown nonce and ASecondReadOfAConsumedNonce_IsRecordedAsAnAnomaly can never pass. A crafter who follows D55 literally reaches 01-03 with a test that cannot go green and no obvious reason why.
risks.mitigation: Resolved in 01-01 by adding a fourth nullable column, HandshakeConsumedAt, and keying the conditional update on it instead of on clearing the hash — which preserves D55's atomicity argument exactly while leaving the row findable. It MUST be decided in 01-01 because it changes the generated migration; discovering it at 01-03 costs a second migration. Flagged as an amendment to a locked decision, to be confirmed by the maintainer rather than absorbed silently.

risks.risk: The signed-in check is written as `User.Identity.AuthenticationType == CookieScheme`. It is the obvious form, it compiles, and it refuses EVERY genuine interactive session — because after an OIDC login the identity reads OpenIdConnect and only the ticket names Cookies. The failure mode is a silent challenge loop, not an exception: the viewer bounces through the identity provider forever and nothing throws.
risks.mitigation: D64, recorded because DISTILL hit it while making the test red, and repeated at the head of 01-02's notes. ViewerEmbedTestHost.ForgeInteractiveSessionCookie deliberately mirrors production (identity type OpenIdConnect, ticket scheme Cookies) so the wrong check fails scenario 7 rather than passing on a test-only shortcut, and scenario 1 is the control proving the forged cookie is a real session in the first place.

risks.risk: The subject validator is wired to ICurrentUserProfileService.GetOrCreateFromPrincipalAsync, which CREATES. That resurrects the profile an administrator just deleted, on that person's very next request, and scenario 17 still passes — the resurrection happens during the request being rejected. The control looks like it works and is a no-op.
risks.mitigation: D57 requires a read-only port with NO create method on the interface, so the convenient service cannot be picked off the container by a later reader. Scenario 18 is the mirror that catches it by issuing a second request. The two seams are deliberately opposite — /embed/start MUST create (scenario 19) and the validator MUST NOT — and 01-02 and 01-04 both say so in those words, because the conflation is the natural reading.

risks.risk: 01-02 is the largest step in the slice: the start endpoint, the grant/refusal write path, a new method on the most security-sensitive service in the codebase, a new configuration value, the terminal pages, and the un-ignoring of scenario 16. It turns only four tests green for that volume of change, which is exactly the ratio at which a crafter starts folding decisions in silently.
risks.mitigation: Its notes carry six named sub-decisions (the authenticate check, the ordering inside the action, the profile-creation asymmetry, the read-only RBAC question, the outcome lifetime, the refusal vocabulary) and three of them are flagged for the commit body. If the diff grows past those, that is the signal to split — and the natural split is the RBAC read method into its own step, which was considered and rejected only because it would then turn zero tests green.

risks.risk: The terminal-page copy is pinned in a Playwright page object and in NO backend test. A typo ships green through the entire backend suite and is caught only in 01-07, which needs a live auth-enabled Lighthouse to run at all — so if that infrastructure is unavailable, the copy has no gate whatsoever and mutation testing will report the constants as survivors.
risks.mitigation: Named as criterion 4 of 01-07 and as an expected mutation survivor in its notes, with the correct fix stated in advance: a backend assertion on the literal, not a shrug. The strings are reproduced verbatim in 01-02's notes so they can be got right at the point of writing rather than at the point of testing.

risks.risk: DQ-2's numbers are proposed, not measured. The 300-second outcome lifetime has never been checked against a real Forge resolver's poll interval, because nobody has one. Too short and the Jira page says `try again` for a sign-in that worked — intermittently, and only for the slowest users, which is the worst possible distribution for a defect.
risks.mitigation: Both clocks are configuration, so the value is changeable without a deploy of new code, and 01-03 makes the enforced window and the advertised window the same by rewriting ExpiresAt at consumption — which removes the class of bug where the two disagree. Flagged for the maintainer in 01-02's notes; the measurement belongs to slice 02, where a real resolver exists.

risks.risk: The refusal-code vocabulary (DQ-1) is unratified and no test pins any string, so it can drift into prose or into an enumeration surface. S14 exists because a refusal that names the reason is a channel that describes the instance to an anonymous caller. The proposed third code's own justification also contradicts scenario 15, which returns 403 for the Blocked licence state and therefore never produces a refusal code at all.
risks.mitigation: Both points are in 01-02's notes with the contradiction stated explicitly and a decision demanded in the commit body. Because no test pins a string, this is settleable at any point in the slice without touching a test — which is the reason DISTILL wrote scenarios 6 and 19 to assert presence rather than value.

risks.risk: The handshake endpoint is unauthenticated and returns a credential, and it cannot be made otherwise under zero-credential install. An attacker who reads the nonce before the legitimate poll consumes it receives the viewer's embed token. The nonce is visible because Atlassian's external-link modal displays the full destination URL on every router.open call, by design and measured — the attacker is not guessing, they are reading.
risks.mitigation: Accepted for a feasibility epic with the blast radius named in full: one session, as one viewer, at most 30 minutes, non-sliding, with NO renewal path (scenario 9 is the test that keeps that true), ended immediately by deleting the user (scenario 17), conferring no other viewer, no durable credential and no write the viewer could not already perform. The design it replaces had an equivalent compromise of everyone who could open the Jira page, permanently, plus a customer credential in a third party's storage. D62 makes the loss OBSERVABLE and is explicitly not a control. This travels forward as an OPEN item; a later slice that stops being about feasibility inherits it unsettled.

risks.risk: No DEVOPS wave has run for this epic, and the four-reviewer gate rejected the demand for one as ceremony — correctly, since there is no new infrastructure and no pipeline change. But the same reasoning means nobody has routed a contract-test recommendation for the one external contract this slice depends on: the identity provider's discovery document and challenge behaviour, which is stubbed at integration level and real only in an E2E that may not run.
risks.mitigation: Recorded, not blocking. The identity provider is the one external, non-deterministic port the architecture says to fake, and only its discovery document is stubbed — the challenge machinery itself stays production. The real coverage is the E2E against real Keycloak, which is why 01-07 treats an unrunnable E2E as a blocked step rather than a skipped one.
